a: A Hymn of the Fathers.
p: The Greek manuscripts head the section 'Hymn of the Fathers'; the Hebrew has 'Praise of the fathers of old'.
b: Swete's Greek opens with a heading, Πατέρων ὕμνος, 'hymn of (the) fathers'. The Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah manuscript B has its own heading on folio XIII verso, line 1: שבח אבות עולם, 'praise of the fathers of old'. From here to 50:24 Ben Sira walks through Israel's story person by person, from Enoch to Nehemiah (44:16–49:13), turns back to the first humans (49:14–16), and ends with the high priest of his own day, Simon (50:1–21). Nothing like this long roll of honor survives from earlier Jewish writing; the closest relatives are later: Mattathias's list in 1 Maccabees 2:51–60 and the roll of faith in Hebrews 11.
orig: Πατέρων ὕμνος (paterōn hymnos), 'hymn of the fathers'

a: men of glory
t: 'Men of glory' or 'men of loyal love'?
p: The Greek praises 'glorious men'; both Hebrew copies say 'men of hesed', men of loyal love.
b: The Greek has ἄνδρας ἐνδόξους, 'men held in glory'. Manuscript B reads אהללה נא אנשי חסד, 'let me praise men of hesed', and the Masada scroll, copied before AD 73, has the same words where it survives (column VII, line 6). Hesed is the covenant word this site renders 'loyal love'. So the Hebrew praises these people first for their faithfulness, the Greek for their fame. The same Hebrew phrase returns in 44:10, where the Greek has 'men of mercy'. The KJV's 'Let us now praise famous men' (KJV) follows the Greek.
orig: ἐνδόξους (endoxous), 'glorious, honored'; Hebrew אנשי חסד ('anshe hesed)

a: The Lord created great glory
t: Glory made, or glory shared out?
p: The Greek says the Lord 'created' glory; the Hebrew says the Most High 'allotted' great glory to them.
b: The Greek πολλὴν δόξαν ἔκτισεν ὁ κύριος means 'the Lord created much glory', with no 'to them'. Manuscript B has רב כבוד חלק להם עליון, 'great glory the Most High shared out to them'. The Hebrew makes the point plain: the fathers' fame was God's gift, not their own achievement. Throughout this part the Greek Kyrios is 'the Lord', because the Greek has no divine name; where the Hebrew stands behind it, manuscript B writes the name YHWH as three yods (ייי), as in 44:16.

a: Some ruled in their kingdoms
p: Kings, counselors, prophets, leaders, scribes, poets and rich men: the list looks like Ben Sira's own world.
b: Before naming anyone, Ben Sira lists the kinds of people he will praise: rulers, advisers, prophets, leaders who shaped the people with plans and writings, composers of songs and poems, and wealthy men at peace (44:3–6). Readers note how closely this matches the ideal scribe of 38:24–39:11, who serves among rulers, travels, studies prophecy and writes. A teacher of young men of good family is holding up models his students could follow. The heroes are almost all men in public life; no woman appears anywhere in 44–50, though Hebrews 11 names Sarah and Rahab.

a: And there are some who are not remembered at all.
p: Ben Sira's hope for the dead is a name that lives on and children who continue. He says nothing here of a life after death.
b: For Ben Sira the worst fate is to vanish 'as if they had never been', with no memory and no line of children. The good live on in two ways: their name is told (44:8, 14–15) and their descendants carry on the covenant (44:11–13). That fits the book as a whole, which nowhere teaches a resurrection (see 17:27–28 and 41:3–4). Here Sirach agrees with much of the Hebrew Bible, where the dead go down to Sheol and a person's name and children are what remain (Psalm 88:10–12; Ecclesiastes 9:5). It stands short of Daniel 12:2 and of 2 Maccabees 7:9, written a generation later, which hope for the dead to rise. Catholic and Orthodox readers read the book within the whole canon, where that hope is clear.

a: men of mercy
p: The Greek 'men of mercy' and manuscript B's 'men of hesed' bracket the opening hymn.
b: Here the Greek uses ἄνδρες ἐλέους, 'men of mercy', where manuscript B again has ואולם אלה אנשי חסד, 'but these were men of loyal love', the same phrase as in 44:1. The Septuagint usually puts eleos, 'mercy', for hesed, so the Greek reader lost the link between 44:1 and 44:10 that the Hebrew reader heard.

a: Their descendants live within the covenants.
p: The Praise of the Fathers is built on God's covenants, one after another.
b: Ben Sira speaks of 'the covenants' in the plural, and the hymn names them in order: with Noah (44:18), Abraham (44:20), Isaac and Jacob (44:22–23), Aaron (45:7, 15), Phinehas (45:24) and David (45:25; 47:11). For him Israel's history is a chain of covenants that God keeps for the sake of the fathers. Where Christians speak of an old and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31; Hebrews 8), Ben Sira's interest is the line of priests and kings these covenants set up.

a: In peace they were buried
p: To be buried in peace, full of years, is the good death the patriarchs were promised.
b: God promised Abraham: "But you yourself will go in peace to your fathers; you will be buried at a good old age" (Genesis 15:15). Ben Sira gives the same blessing to all his heroes. Burial mattered: the bones of Joseph (49:15) and the bones of the judges and the prophets (46:12; 49:10) come up again in the hymn.

a: the assembly
p: The Greek ekklēsia here is Israel gathered for worship, not the later Christian church.
b: The word is ἐκκλησία, which the Septuagint uses for the Hebrew qahal, Israel assembled before God. The New Testament took it over for the church. In Ben Sira it means the worshiping congregation, the same assembly that stands before Simon in 50:13 and 50:20.

a: Enoch pleased the Lord and was carried off
p: Ben Sira begins and ends his list with Enoch, using the Greek verb that Hebrews 11:5 also uses.
b: Genesis says only: "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). The Greek of Ben Sira, like the Septuagint of Genesis, says he 'pleased' the Lord and was 'carried off' (μετετέθη). Hebrews takes up the same words: "By faith Enoch was carried off, so that he did not see death" (Hebrews 11:5). Manuscript B has the Hebrew of Genesis: Enoch 'walked with the LORD and was taken'. Enoch returns at 49:14. The verse is missing from the Masada scroll (see the variant on this verse), and readers have asked whether it was added later so that the list begins and ends with him.

a: the exchange
p: The Greek calls Noah an antallagma, something given in exchange; the Hebrew calls him a tachalif, a replacement.
b: The Greek ἀντάλλαγμα means a thing given in place of another, a ransom or substitute. Manuscript B has לעת כלה היה תחליף, 'in the time of destruction he became a replacement': Noah's family took the place of the world that perished and gave humanity a new start. Genesis says, "Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his generations" (Genesis 6:9). Christian readers later saw in Noah's rescue a picture of baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21), but the verse itself is about a new beginning for the human race.

a: With him covenants were made that last forever
p: God's promise after the flood was that 'all flesh' would never again be cut off by flood.
b: Ben Sira retells Genesis 9: "All flesh will not again be cut off by the waters of the flood" (Genesis 9:11). Manuscript B says the covenant was made 'with an everlasting sign' (באות עולם), the rainbow of Genesis 9:12–17. The Greek has 'covenants', plural, matching the plural of 44:11.

a: father of a multitude of nations
p: Ben Sira echoes the renaming of Abram in Genesis 17.
b: God told Abram, "Abraham will be your name, because I have made you father of a multitude of nations" (Genesis 17:5). For Ben Sira, Abraham's glory is unmatched; manuscript B adds that God 'put no blemish on his glory'. Paul builds on the same verse to argue that Abraham is the father of believing Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 4:16–17).

a: He guarded the law of the Most High
p: Ben Sira says Abraham kept the law, was circumcised and passed the test. Paul stresses that his faith came before circumcision and the law.
b: Ben Sira joins three things: Abraham kept the law of the Most High, received the covenant in his flesh (circumcision, Genesis 17:10–14) and was found faithful when tested (Genesis 22:1). He can say Abraham kept the law, long before Sinai, because God said Abraham "kept what I required of him: my commands, my rules and my laws" (Genesis 26:5). 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (1 Maccabees 2:52), and James 2:21–23 also ties Abraham's faith to his deeds. Paul reads the story in a different order: Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised (Romans 4:9–11), and the law came 430 years later (Galatians 3:17). Here Ben Sira agrees with Genesis and James and differs in emphasis from Paul.
r: Genesis 17:10–14; Genesis 22:1; Genesis 26:5; 1 Maccabees 2:52; James 2:21–23; Romans 4:9–11; Galatians 3:17

a: he bound himself to him with an oath
t: The oath after the binding of Isaac
p: The promise of 44:21 comes from Genesis 22, after Abraham's test, and ends with words from Psalm 72.
b: The oath is the one God swore after the binding of Isaac: "By myself I swear, says the LORD" (Genesis 22:16), with its promise of offspring like the stars and blessing for the nations (Genesis 22:17–18). Ben Sira adds the dust of the earth from Genesis 13:16 and closes with the borders of the ideal king in Psalm 72:8, "from the River to the ends of the earth" (Psalm 72:8). 'The River' is the Euphrates. He has turned the patriarch's promise into a picture of Israel's widest hopes.

a: he made them rest on the head of Jacob
p: Manuscript B's copyist wrote another reading in the margin: 'he gave him the birthright'.
b: In manuscript B, folio XIV recto, line 11, the main text reads 'he established him with a blessing', and the margin offers 'he named him with the birthright' (ויכנהו בבכורה). Copyists of the Genizah manuscripts often noted other readings this way, which shows that more than one Hebrew text of Ben Sira was in circulation in the Middle Ages. The Greek follows neither exactly. Both readings recall Jacob taking Esau's birthright and blessing (Genesis 25:29–34; 27:1–40).

a: a man of mercy
p: The chapter break falls in the middle of a sentence: the 'man of mercy' is Moses, named in 45:1.
b: The Greek sentence that begins 'From him he brought out a man of mercy' continues into 45:1, where Moses is named. Manuscript B runs on the same way. Chapter divisions were added to the Bible in the Middle Ages, long after the book was written, and here the break cuts a thought in two.

a: whose memory is spoken with blessings
p: Manuscript B says 'Moses, may his memory be for good', close to the Jewish phrase still said of the dead.
b: The Greek οὗ τὸ μνημόσυνον ἐν εὐλογίαις means 'whose memory is in blessings'. Manuscript B has משה זכרו לטובה, 'Moses, his memory for good', like Nehemiah's prayer 'remember me for good'. Jews today say of a person who has died, 'may his memory be a blessing'. Ben Sira says the same of the judges (46:11).

a: loved by God and by people
t: Moses honored by God and people
p: Exodus says Moses was held in honor even in Egypt.
b: The phrase sums up the Moses of Exodus: God spoke with him as a friend (Exodus 33:11), and "The man Moses was also held in high honor in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 11:3). Moses gets only five verses in Ben Sira's hymn, Aaron seventeen (45:6–22). See the note on 45:6.

a: the holy ones
t: Like the holy ones, or like God?
p: The Greek compares Moses with 'the holy ones' (angels). Manuscript B, damaged here, has the word Elohim, 'God'.
b: The Greek reads ὡμοίωσεν αὐτὸν δόξῃ ἁγίων, 'he made him like the holy ones in glory', meaning the angels. Manuscript B is damaged at the start of the line (folio XIV recto, line 15), but the word אלהים, Elohim, is legible. In Hebrew that can mean 'God' or 'divine beings'. Exodus twice says Moses would be 'as God': to Aaron, "you will become as God to him" (Exodus 4:16), and to Pharaoh, "See, I have set you as God to Pharaoh" (Exodus 7:1). The Greek translator may have softened a bold phrase.

a: By his words he made the signs stop
t: Plagues that stopped at Moses' word
p: The 'signs' are the plagues of Egypt, which ended when Moses prayed.
b: Several plagues ended when Moses spoke to God: the frogs (Exodus 8:12–13), the flies (Exodus 8:30–31), the hail (Exodus 9:33) and the locusts (Exodus 10:18–19). The Greek verb katepausen means 'made to cease'. The KJV and some modern versions understand the line instead as 'he caused signs to happen quickly'; the Greek supports 'stop'.

a: faithful and humble
p: Ben Sira takes both words from Numbers 12.
b: When Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, the narrator said: "Now the man Moses was very humble, more than any human being on the face of the ground" (Numbers 12:3), and God said: "In all my house he is faithful" (Numbers 12:7). Ben Sira values the same two virtues in his students (1:27; 3:17–18).

a: the deep darkness
p: Moses went into the darkness on Sinai where God was.
b: Ben Sira retells Exodus 20: "So the people kept their distance, and Moses went up close to the deep darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21). 'Face to face' recalls Exodus 33:11, "The LORD spoke to Moses face to face," and Deuteronomy 34:10. Later Christian writers on prayer took Moses' entry into the darkness as a picture of drawing near to a God beyond human sight.

a: the law of life and knowledge
p: Manuscript B calls it 'the law of life and understanding', a phrase Ben Sira also uses in 17:11.
b: Greek νόμον ζωῆς καὶ ἐπιστήμης; Hebrew תורת חיים ותבונה, 'a law of life and understanding'. For Ben Sira the law of Moses is the very form wisdom takes in Israel (24:23). The idea goes back to Deuteronomy 30:15–20, where the commandments are set before Israel as life and death.

a: He lifted Aaron high
p: Aaron gets more than three times the space given to Moses. The hymn is building toward the high priest Simon in chapter 50.
b: Ben Sira gives Moses five verses (44:23–45:5) and Aaron seventeen (45:6–22), with three more for Phinehas. Historians see in this the outlook of a Jerusalem scribe who admired the temple priesthood: the priestly vestments of 45:8–13 come back on Simon in 50:11, with the same Greek words. Some suggest Ben Sira was himself a priest; one hand of Codex Sinaiticus calls him 'the priest' in 50:27 (see the variant there), but the book never says so. Jewish and Christian readers alike see here the high honor of Aaron's line in Second Temple Judaism, before the priesthood fell into dispute under the Seleucids and the Maccabees.

a: the undershorts, the long robe and the ephod
p: Ben Sira names the high priest's garments from Exodus 28.
b: Exodus lists "a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a tunic of checkered weave, a turban and a sash" (Exodus 28:4), and adds linen undershorts (Exodus 28:42). The 'long robe' (podērēs, 'reaching to the feet') is the Septuagint's word for the robe of the ephod. Revelation 1:13 dresses the risen Christ in the same podērēs, and Christian readers have long heard a priestly picture there.

a: gold bells
p: The bells told those outside when the high priest moved in the holy place.
b: Exodus 28:33–35 sets pomegranates and gold bells around the hem, "a gold bell and a pomegranate, a gold bell and a pomegranate, all around the hem of the robe" (Exodus 28:34), and says, "Its sound will be heard when he goes into the holy place before the LORD and when he comes out, and so he will not die" (Exodus 28:35). Ben Sira turns the sound into 'a reminder' for the people: manuscript B has לזכרון לבני עמו, 'for a remembrance for the children of his people'.

a: the tokens of truth
p: The Greek 'tokens of truth' is the Septuagint's way of naming the Urim and Thummim, the high priest's lots for seeking God's decision.
b: The Greek λογίῳ κρίσεως, δήλοις ἀληθείας means 'the oracle of judgment, the clear signs of truth'. The first phrase is the Septuagint's name for the breastpiece, which this site calls "the breastpiece for decisions" (Exodus 28:15). The second goes back to the Septuagint's rendering of Urim and Thummim as 'showing and truth' (see 1 Esdras 5:40). Exodus says: "Put the Urim and the Thummim into the breastpiece for decisions" (Exodus 28:30). Manuscript B lists here 'the breastpiece of judgment, ephod and sash' and does not mention the Urim.
orig: δήλοις ἀληθείας (dēlois alētheias), 'clear signs of truth'

a: precious stones cut like seals
p: Each stone on the breastpiece carried the name of a tribe.
b: Exodus 28:17–21 sets twelve precious stones in four rows, engraved like seals, each with the name of one of the sons of Israel. Ben Sira calls the engraving 'a reminder': the high priest carried the tribes before God. Revelation 21:19–20 takes up a similar list of twelve stones for the foundations of the new Jerusalem.

a: engraved like a holy seal
p: Exodus calls it a plate engraved 'Holy to the LORD'; Ben Sira calls it a gold crown.
b: Exodus has: "Make a plate of pure gold. Engrave on it, as a seal is engraved, 'Holy to the LORD.'" (Exodus 28:36). Ben Sira calls it a 'gold crown' (stephanos) on the turban, and the Greek speaks only of 'the engraving of a seal of holiness'. Manuscript B has the Hebrew word tsits (ציץ), the 'plate' or 'flower' of Exodus 28:36, followed by a gap and the word 'holiness'. By Ben Sira's time the high priest wore this plate like a king's diadem.

a: an outsider
p: Only Aaron's descendants could wear these garments.
b: The Greek ἀλλογενὴς means 'one of another family'. Manuscript B has zar, the word this site renders 'outsider': anyone not of Aaron's line. Numbers says the bronze plating of the altar was "a reminder for the Israelites... No outsider, no one who is not of Aaron's offspring, was to come near to burn incense before the LORD" (Numbers 16:40). The point sets up the story of Korah in 45:18–19.

a: twice a day without fail
p: The Greek speaks of the daily burnt offering; manuscript B of the high priest's grain offering. Both were made morning and evening.
b: Israel offered "two yearling lambs, every day, without fail" (Exodus 29:38), one in the morning and one at dusk. Manuscript B has instead 'his grain offering is burned whole', the high priest's own grain offering of Leviticus 6:19–23: "a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening" (Leviticus 6:20). The daily service is the setting many readers find in Simon's scene in 50:11–21.

a: installed him as priest
p: Greek and Hebrew both use the old idiom 'Moses filled his hands', which means to ordain a priest.
b: The Greek ἐπλήρωσεν Μωυσῆς τὰς χεῖρας and manuscript B's וימלא משה את ידו both say 'Moses filled his hand(s)'. The phrase is the Hebrew Bible's term for ordaining a priest (Exodus 29:9; Leviticus 8:33), perhaps from placing the first offerings in his hands. The Plain gives the sense.
orig: ἐπλήρωσεν τὰς χεῖρας (eplērōsen tas cheiras), 'filled the hands'

a: to bless his people in the name
p: Aaron's sons were to bless Israel with God's name, as in the Priestly Blessing.
b: After the Priestly Blessing God says: "So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I myself will bless them" (Numbers 6:27). Manuscript B reads 'to bless his people in his name' (בשמו). The scene comes alive in 50:20, where Simon raises his hands and blesses the people.

a: a token portion
p: The Greek 'memorial' is the Septuagint's word for the azkarah, the part of an offering burned on the altar.
b: The Greek has εἰς μνημόσυνον, 'for a memorial', and manuscript B has ואזכרה, the azkarah of Leviticus 2, which this site calls the 'token portion': "He is to make this token portion go up in smoke on the altar" (Leviticus 2:2). The Greek rendering points to the idea behind the word: the offering 'reminds' God.

a: for your people
p: The Greek turns to address God for a moment: 'your people'.
b: The Greek ends ἐξιλάσκεσθαι περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ σου, 'to make atonement for your people'. Swete's notes say the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus lacks 'your' (a corrector added it), and manuscript B has 'for the Israelites'. The shift to speaking to God is like a hymn breaking into prayer.
orig: τοῦ λαοῦ σου (tou laou sou), 'your people'

a: Outsiders banded together against him
p: Ben Sira calls Korah and his allies 'outsiders' because they claimed a priesthood that was not theirs.
b: Numbers 16 tells how Korah, a Levite, with Dathan and Abiram of Reuben, rose against Moses and Aaron. Ben Sira calls them allotrioi, 'outsiders' (manuscript B: zarim), because they wanted the priesthood that belonged to Aaron alone (see 45:13). Jude 11 names 'Korah's rebellion' as a warning to the church.

a: ate them up with the flame of his fire
p: Fire from the Lord burned up the men who offered incense without right.
b: "And fire came out from the LORD and ate up the two hundred fifty men who were offering the incense" (Numbers 16:35). The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:31–33); Ben Sira mentions only the fire. The 'strange signs' are the new thing God created in Numbers 16:30.

a: the firstfruits of the first crops
p: Priests owned no land; they lived on the firstfruits and the sacrifices.
b: Numbers 18:12–19 gives Aaron's family the best of the oil, wine and grain, the firstfruits and the holy portions. Ben Sira had already told his students to honor the priests and give them their share 'as you were commanded' (7:29–31). In his day these dues supported a large priestly class in Jerusalem.

a: for he himself is your share, your inheritance
t: The Lord as the priests' share
p: Ben Sira quotes the promise to Aaron in Numbers 18:20.
b: God told Aaron: "You will have no inheritance in their land, and no portion among them will be yours. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). The Greek's 'your' keeps the words of God's address to Aaron.

a: Third in glory comes Phinehas son of Eleazar
p: Phinehas stopped a plague by his zeal and received a covenant of priesthood. The Maccabees later held him up as their model.
b: In Numbers 25 Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman at Peor, and the plague stopped. God said: "Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned my rage back from the Israelites" (Numbers 25:11), and promised "a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites" (Numbers 25:13). A generation after Ben Sira, Mattathias began the Maccabean revolt "as Phinehas did" (1 Maccabees 2:26) and called him "Phinehas our father" (1 Maccabees 2:54). Zeal for the law, praised here, became the banner of armed resistance.

a: a covenant of peace
t: The high priesthood for Phinehas's line
p: Manuscript B says the covenant gave Phinehas's family 'the high priesthood forever', the line of Zadok and of Simon.
b: Numbers 25:12 has "I am giving him my covenant: peace", and Malachi recalls Levi: "Life and peace were my covenant with him" (Malachi 2:5). Where the Greek has 'the greatness of the priesthood', manuscript B has כהונה גדולה עד עולם, 'high priesthood forever'. The high priests of Jerusalem, Zadok's line, traced their descent through Phinehas (1 Chronicles 6:4–8), and so did Simon (50:1). Ben Sira's prayer at 50:24 in the Hebrew asks God to keep 'the covenant of Phinehas' with Simon.

a: the inheritance of a king goes from one son to one son
p: The line sets the priestly covenant beside the royal one. Readers differ on what the comparison means.
b: The Greek contrasts the two: a king's inheritance passes from one son to one son, while Aaron's belongs to his whole line. Manuscript B is obscure here ('the inheritance of a man before his glory', or with other vowels 'of fire'). One reading sees the priesthood as broader and more secure than kingship, which fits a time with no Davidic king, when the high priest led the Jews. Another sees Ben Sira honoring both covenants equally and keeping hope for David's line alive (compare 47:11 and 47:22). Christian readers have joined the two in Christ, who is both king (Luke 1:32–33) and priest (Hebrews 7).

a: May he put wisdom in your hearts
p: Ben Sira blesses the priests of his own day. Manuscript B first adds a call to bless the LORD.
b: The 'you' is plural: the priests, Aaron's heirs, who judged and taught the people in Ben Sira's day. Manuscript B, folio XV verso, line 7, has a line the Greek lacks: ועתה ברכו נא את ייי הטוב 'And now bless the LORD, the good one', 'who crowns you with glory'. The same call, 'And now bless', closes the portrait of Simon (50:22). The hymn's two great sections end with blessings on the priests.
orig: δῴη ὑμῖν (dōē hymin), 'may he give you' (plural)

a: Joshua son of Nun
p: In Greek Joshua is Iēsous, the same name as Jesus and as Ben Sira himself.
b: The Greek Ἰησοῦς Ναυή is 'Jesus son of Nave', the Septuagint's form of 'Joshua son of Nun'. Hebrew Yehoshua means 'the LORD saves', and Ben Sira plays on it: 'he lived up to his name, great in rescuing'. The same Greek name belongs to the author (50:27; 51:1) and to Jeshua the priest (49:12). The New Testament uses the play too: "Name him Jesus, for he is the one who will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21), and Hebrews 4:8 calls Joshua 'Jesus'.

a: Moses' successor in prophecy
p: Ben Sira counts Joshua among the prophets. Manuscript B calls him Moses' 'attendant in prophecy'.
b: The Greek διάδοχος Μωσῆ ἐν προφητείαις makes Joshua Moses' successor in prophecy. Manuscript B has משרת משה בנבואה, 'Moses' attendant in prophecy', the word Exodus uses: "But his servant Joshua son of Nun, a young man, never left the inside of the tent" (Exodus 33:11). In the Jewish Bible the books from Joshua to Kings are 'the Former Prophets', and Ben Sira's hymn moves through them in order.

a: turned his sword against the cities
p: The Greek says 'sword'; manuscript B has the javelin Joshua held out against Ai.
b: The Greek has ῥομφαίαν, 'sword'. Manuscript B reads בהניפו כידון על עיר, 'when he waved a javelin against a city', recalling Ai: "So Joshua held out the javelin in his hand toward the town" (Joshua 8:18). Joshua kept it stretched out until the town was destroyed (Joshua 8:26), like Moses' raised hands in Exodus 17:11.

a: The Lord himself led the enemy to him
p: Manuscript B gives the reason differently: 'for the wars of the LORD' he fought.
b: Where the Greek says the Lord brought the enemies, manuscript B has 'for the wars of the LORD', followed by a damaged word (folio XV verso, line 13). The phrase recalls 'the Book of the Wars of the LORD' (Numbers 21:14) and the conviction of Joshua 10:14 that "the LORD fought for Israel" (Joshua 10:14). Ben Sira, writing for students in a peaceful city, presents Joshua's wars as God's own.

a: the sun stepped back
p: Ben Sira reads Joshua 10 as a true stopping of the sun, and uses the same Greek verb for Hezekiah's sign in 48:23.
b: Joshua 10:12–14 tells how the sun stood still at Gibeon: "There has never been a day like that one, before it or after it, when the LORD listened to a man's voice" (Joshua 10:14). The Greek verb ἀνεπόδισεν, 'went back, stepped back', returns at 48:23 for the sun going back in Hezekiah's day, so the two miracles are linked. Manuscript B has the verb of Joshua 10:13, 'the sun stood still' (עמד השמש). How to read the miracle is discussed on the topic page.

a: the Most High Sovereign
p: Ben Sira gives God the title dynastēs, 'ruler, sovereign', here and in 46:6 and 46:16.
b: The Greek τὸν ὕψιστον δυνάστην joins 'Most High' with dynastēs, 'the one who holds power'. 2 Maccabees uses it often of God, and Mary uses the word for the rulers God brings down (Luke 1:52); 1 Timothy 6:15 calls God 'the blessed and only Sovereign'. Manuscript B has 'God Most High' (אל עליון), and the hailstones recall Joshua 10:11.

a: their full armor
p: The Greek panoplia, 'full armor', is the word of Ephesians 6. Manuscript B speaks instead of 'every nation under the ban'.
b: The Greek πανοπλίαν αὐτῶν means 'their complete armor'. Paul uses the word for 'all of God's armor' (Ephesians 6:11, 13). Manuscript B has למען דעת כל גוי חרם, 'so that every nation of the ban might know', using cherem, the ban that devoted Canaan's cities to destruction (Joshua 6:17). The Greek translator may have read the letters differently. The line ends in manuscript B 'for he followed God fully', the words said of Caleb in Numbers 14:24.

a: he and Caleb son of Jephunneh
p: Joshua and Caleb urged Israel to trust God and enter the land, when the other spies spread fear.
b: Numbers 13–14 tells how ten spies brought back a bad report and the people grumbled, while Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and pleaded with them (Numbers 14:6–9). God said: "But my servant Caleb had a different spirit with him, and he followed me fully" (Numbers 14:24). Manuscript B says they stood 'when the assembly broke loose' (בפרע קהל); the Greek has 'against the enemy'.

a: only these two came through safe
t: Two out of six hundred thousand
p: Of the adults who left Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb entered the land.
b: Moses counted "six hundred thousand men on foot" (Numbers 11:21). God swore that none of that generation would enter the land except Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:30, 38; 26:65). 'A land flowing with milk and honey' is the phrase of Exodus 3:8.

a: strength that lasted into his old age
p: Caleb said at eighty-five that he was as strong as on the day Moses sent him.
b: Caleb claimed Hebron saying: "I am as strong now as I was then, strong enough for war and for going out and coming back" (Joshua 14:11). His family held it after him (Joshua 14:13–15; 15:13–19).

a: each by his own name
p: Ben Sira honors the judges as a group and names none of them, only those who stayed faithful.
b: Ben Sira praises 'the judges', with a condition: only those whose hearts did not 'play the prostitute' and did not turn from the Lord. The image is the one Judges uses for Gideon's ephod: "All Israel went after it there like a prostitute" (Judges 8:27). Hebrews 11:32 names Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah; Ben Sira names none, and readers have wondered whether the condition was meant to leave some out.

a: May their bones sprout again from their place
p: The same wish is made for the Twelve Prophets in 49:10. It may express hope that their memory and their line will live, or something more.
b: The image comes from Isaiah: "your bones will sprout like new grass" (Isaiah 66:14). Ben Sira's second line explains it: their name passes to their sons. Most readers take it as a wish that the judges' memory stay fresh, in line with the book's silence about a resurrection (see 44:9). Others hear a hint of the hope of Ezekiel 37 and Isaiah 26:19, that the dead will live. The same wish recurs for the Twelve Prophets in 49:10, where the manuscripts and the Twelve are discussed.

a: the Lord's prophet
p: Manuscript B gives Samuel three titles: 'Nazirite of the LORD in prophecy', 'judge' and 'priest'.
b: Manuscript B, folio XVI recto, line 12, reads שמואל שופט ומכהן, 'Samuel, judge and priest', and before it 'a Nazirite of the LORD in prophecy'. Samuel's mother vowed that no razor would touch his head (1 Samuel 1:11), and he offered sacrifices (1 Samuel 7:9), though he was not of Aaron's line (1 Chronicles 6:33–34 lists him among the Levites of Kohath). Ben Sira's Samuel is the bridge between the judges and the kings. "Everyone in Israel, from Dan all the way to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was proven trustworthy as a prophet of the LORD" (1 Samuel 3:20).

a: the Lord came to the help of Jacob
p: The verb means God came to look after his people, as in Genesis 50:25.
b: The Greek ἐπεσκέψατο, 'visited, looked after', renders the Hebrew paqad, used when God steps in to help, as in Joseph's last words: "God will surely come to help you" (Genesis 50:25). The same verb is used of Joseph's bones in 49:15 and of God visiting his people in Luke 1:68.

a: a reliable seer
p: Manuscript B calls Samuel a ro'eh, 'seer', the older name for a prophet.
b: The Greek πιστὸς ὁράσεως means 'faithful in vision'. Manuscript B has וגם בדברו נאמן רועה, 'and by his word he was trustworthy as a seer'. 1 Samuel 9:9 explains that a prophet used to be called a seer, and Samuel is 'the seer' of that chapter.

a: a lamb still nursing
p: Ben Sira retells 1 Samuel 7, where God answered Samuel's sacrifice with thunder.
b: "Samuel took a lamb still nursing and offered it up whole to the LORD as a burnt offering. Samuel called out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him" (1 Samuel 7:9).

a: The Lord thundered out of heaven
p: The thunder of 1 Samuel 7:10 threw the Philistines into confusion.
b: "That day the LORD thundered over the Philistines with a great voice" (1 Samuel 7:10). Hannah's song had promised it: the LORD thunders from heaven against his enemies (1 Samuel 2:10).

a: Money, even sandals, I have taken from no one.
p: Ben Sira retells Samuel's farewell in 1 Samuel 12, where no one could accuse him of taking a bribe.
b: Samuel asked Israel: "From whose hand did I take a bribe to look the other way?" (1 Samuel 12:3), and they answered that he had taken nothing (1 Samuel 12:4–5). Manuscript B has כופר ונעלם, 'a bribe' and a word whose letters can be read ne'lam, 'something hidden' (Abegg and Parker: 'secret gift'), or na'alayim, 'a pair of sandals', which is how the Greek takes it. A pair of sandals stood for a small bribe in Amos 2:6 and 8:6. Ben Sira, who warns his students against bribes (20:29), holds Samuel up as the honest judge.

a: After he had gone to sleep in death, he still prophesied.
p: Ben Sira takes it as fact that the dead Samuel himself spoke to Saul at Endor.
b: 1 Samuel 28 tells how Saul had a medium call up Samuel, who said: "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me" (1 Samuel 28:19). Ben Sira, about 180 BC, reads this plainly: Samuel prophesied after death 'from the earth'. Manuscript B says 'even after his death he was sought' (נדרש). Later Jewish and Christian readers argued whether it was really Samuel, a demon or a trick, and whether such a consultation could ever be right (1 Chronicles 10:13 condemns Saul for it). Whether the faithful dead can hear or help the living is asked on the card at 1 Samuel 28.

a: Next came Nathan
t: Nathan, the prophet of David's court
p: Between Samuel and Elijah Ben Sira names only one prophet: Nathan.
b: Nathan brought David God's promise of a lasting house (2 Samuel 7:1–17) and his rebuke after Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:1–15), and he helped make Solomon king (1 Kings 1). Ben Sira passes over Gad and the other court prophets. Nathan's place here, just before David, marks him as the voice that framed David's reign.

a: As the fat is lifted off the peace offering
t: David like the fat of the offering
p: The fat of a peace offering was set apart for God alone. So David was the part of Israel God claimed as his own.
b: In a peace offering the worshiper ate most of the meat, but the fat was burned on the altar: "All the fat belongs to the LORD" (Leviticus 3:16). Manuscript B has כי כחלב מורם מקדש, 'like fat lifted from the holy offering'. The comparison is a priest's way of saying 'the choicest part': David was the best of Israel, set aside for God.

a: Lions were his playthings
p: David told Saul he had killed lions and bears that attacked his flock.
b: David said he struck down lions and bears to save his father's sheep (1 Samuel 17:34–36). Ben Sira makes the danger a game: David played with lions as if they were young goats. Manuscript B compares the bears to 'the young of Bashan', the rich grazing land east of the Jordan.

a: a giant
p: The Greek gigas is the Septuagint's word for the Nephilim and other giants.
b: The Greek calls Goliath γίγαντα, a 'giant', the word the Septuagint uses for the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4. Manuscript B has simply gibbor, 'warrior' (גבור). 1 Samuel 17 tells the story, and 'the people's disgrace' is the taunt Goliath threw at Israel's army (1 Samuel 17:10, 26).

a: lift up the horn of his people
p: A horn stands for strength and victory, like the horns of a wild bull.
b: Hannah sang that God would "raise high his anointed one's horn" (1 Samuel 2:10), and Zechariah praised God for raising "a horn of salvation" in David's house (Luke 1:69). Ben Sira uses the image four times in this chapter (47:5, 7, 11) and again in 49:5.

a: his tens of thousands
p: The women sang that David had struck his tens of thousands.
b: After Goliath fell the women sang: "Saul has struck his thousands, / David his tens of thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7). That song made Saul jealous; Ben Sira keeps only its praise, and adds the 'glorious crown' of David's kingship.

a: it stays broken to this day
t: The Philistines in Ben Sira's day
p: David broke Philistine power, and Ben Sira still counts their heirs among Israel's foes.
b: David defeated the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:17–25; 8:1). In Ben Sira's time the old Philistine coast held Greek cities such as Gaza and Ashdod, and in 50:26 he names 'the Philistines' among the nations he loathes. 'To this day' reads David's victory as still standing.

a: With his whole heart he sang hymns
p: Ben Sira's David is the psalm singer of the book of Psalms and the organizer of temple music in Chronicles.
b: Many psalms carry David's name in their titles, and his last words call him "the darling of Israel's songs" (2 Samuel 23:1). Ben Sira joins that picture with the David of Chronicles, who set up the temple singers (47:9). Manuscript B says 'in all his deeds he gave thanks' (בכל מעשהו נתן הודות).

a: psalm singers in front of the altar
p: Chronicles says David appointed Levites to sing and play before the ark and in the temple.
b: 1 Chronicles 16:4–6 has David appoint Levites to give thanks and praise before the ark, and 1 Chronicles 25 organizes the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun into twenty-four courses of singers. Ben Sira, who knew the temple's music firsthand (50:18), traces it back to David.

a: set their seasons in order
p: Chronicles credits David with ordering the Levites' service for sabbaths, new moons and feasts.
b: 1 Chronicles 23:30–31 has the Levites stand every morning and evening to praise the LORD, and at every burnt offering on sabbaths, new moons and set feasts. Ben Sira's 'from dawn' matches that morning praise. The Greek 'until the cycle was complete' (mechri synteleias) may mean through the whole year.

a: His sins the Lord removed
p: Ben Sira mentions David's sins and God's forgiveness, without telling the story of Bathsheba.
b: When Nathan confronted him, "David said to Nathan, 'I have sinned against the LORD.' Nathan said to David, 'The LORD, for his part, has put away your sin. You will not die.'" (2 Samuel 12:13). Chronicles leaves the story out; Ben Sira names the sin in a word and moves on to the promise.

a: a covenant of kings
p: God promised David a house and a throne that would last.
b: 2 Samuel 7:12–16 promises David a son on his throne and a kingdom forever, and Psalm 89 calls it a covenant. Ben Sira speaks of 'a covenant of kings' and 'a throne of glory'. Whether he looked for a coming king from David's line is discussed at 47:22.

a: A son full of knowledge
p: Manuscript B calls Solomon 'a wise son' (ben maskil) who 'dwelt in safety'.
b: The Greek υἱὸς ἐπιστήμων means 'a son with understanding'. Manuscript B has 'a wise son' and says he 'lived in security' (שוכן לבטח). Solomon reaped what David had won: the wars were over, and he could build.

a: Solomon's reign was a time of peace
p: Solomon's name sounds like shalom, 'peace', and Chronicles makes the link.
b: God told David: "Solomon will be his name, and in his days I will give Israel peace and calm" (1 Chronicles 22:9). Ben Sira's 'a time of peace' and 'quiet on every border' follow that promise, and the 'house for his name' is the temple of 1 Kings 6–8.

a: like a river in flood
p: Manuscript B says Solomon overflowed 'like the Nile'.
b: The Greek has 'like a river'. Manuscript B reads ותצף כיאר מוסר, 'you overflowed like the Nile with instruction', using ye'or, the word for the Nile in Genesis 41:1. The Nile flooded every year and watered all of Egypt; so Solomon's wisdom spread over the world. Ben Sira uses the same picture of the law in 24:25–27.

a: riddling proverbs
p: 1 Kings says Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs and wrote over a thousand songs.
b: "Three thousand proverbs came from his lips, and there were one thousand and five of his songs" (1 Kings 4:32). The queen of Sheba "came to put him to the test with riddles" (1 Kings 10:1). Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes were linked with his name; the Wisdom of Solomon was later written in it.

a: the distant islands
p: 'The islands' means the coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean, the edge of the known world.
b: The word is the one this site renders 'the islands' in Isaiah and Ezekiel: the far western coasts and islands of the sea. 1 Kings 4:34 says people came from every nation to hear Solomon's wisdom.

a: as though it were tin
t: Gold and silver, wives and horses
p: Ben Sira praises Solomon's wealth, then turns to his downfall in the next verse. Deuteronomy's law for kings forbade both.
b: "In Jerusalem the king made silver like the stones" (1 Kings 10:27). Ben Sira compares it to tin and lead, cheap metals. Deuteronomy's law for kings says: "He must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside. And he must not pile up great amounts of silver and gold for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:17). Ben Sira sets Solomon's gold (47:18) and his wives (47:19) side by side, the two things that law warned against.

a: who is called the God of Israel
p: Manuscript B speaks of Solomon himself: 'you were called by the glorious name that is called over Israel'.
b: The Greek speaks of 'the Lord God, who is called the God of Israel'. Manuscript B has נקראת בשם הנכבד, 'you were called by the honored name', 'which is called over Israel'. That may point to Solomon's other name, Jedidiah, 'loved by the LORD' (2 Samuel 12:25), which carries God's name. The Greek moves the name from Solomon to God.

a: you gave your loins to women
p: Solomon's many wives turned his heart to other gods, as 1 Kings 11 says.
b: "Seven hundred wives belonged to him, women of noble rank, and three hundred concubines. His wives bent his heart away" (1 Kings 11:3). Nehemiah 13:26 used Solomon as the great warning against marrying foreign women. Ben Sira, who is often hard on women elsewhere in the book, here places the blame on Solomon: 'you gave', 'you marred'.

a: I was stung with grief at your folly
p: The Greek verb is 'I was stung'; manuscript B has 'groaning over your bed'.
b: Swete's Greek has κατενύγην, first person: 'I was pierced', as if Ben Sira himself mourns. Manuscript B has 'and groaning over your bed' (ואנחה על משכבך), the bed meaning his offspring. The KJV, from another Greek text, has 'they were grieved'. Either way the result follows in 47:21: the kingdom split.

a: from Ephraim a rebel kingdom began
p: After Solomon the ten northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam, about 930 BC.
b: 1 Kings 12 tells how Rehoboam refused to lighten the people's load and the north rejected him. Ben Sira calls the northern kingdom 'rebel' (apeithēs, 'disobedient'). His hostility to the north continues in his day toward 'the foolish people who live in Shechem' (50:26).

a: a root that came from him
t: A root for David: a hope for a messiah?
p: God's promise to David cannot fail, says Ben Sira. Readers differ on whether he looked for a coming son of David.
b: Ben Sira echoes 2 Samuel 7:15, "But my loyal love will not turn away from him", and Isaiah's "root of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:10). Some read here a real hope for a king from David's line, which Jews and Christians later called the Messiah. Others note that Ben Sira says little else about it: the leaders he praises in his own day are priests (45:24–25; 50:1–21). The Hebrew psalm after 51:12 in manuscript B thanks God 'who makes a horn sprout for the house of David'. Christians read the root of David as Jesus (Romans 15:12; Revelation 5:5).

a: the folly of the people
p: Manuscript B calls Rehoboam 'broad in folly', a play on his name, which means 'the people is broad'.
b: The name Rehoboam (Rechav'am) means 'the people is broad'. Manuscript B writes רחב אולת וחסר בינה, 'broad of folly and lacking understanding'. The Greek keeps half the pun: 'the folly of the people' (λαοῦ ἀφροσύνην). Manuscript B also curses Jeroboam's memory, 'may he have no memory' (אל יהי לו זכר), the opposite of the blessed memory of 45:1 and 46:11.

a: who made Israel sin
p: Kings repeats that Jeroboam 'made Israel sin' by setting up golden calves.
b: Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30), and Kings judges every later northern king by it: God "will give Israel up because of the sins Jeroboam committed, the sins he made Israel commit" (1 Kings 14:16).

a: until they were driven out of their land
t: The fall of the northern kingdom
p: Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC and deported its people.
b: 2 Kings 17 explains the fall of Israel as the result of its sins, from Jeroboam's calves onward. Ben Sira gives it in two lines, and returns to it in 48:15, after Elijah and Elisha, in words close to 2 Kings 17:7–23.

a: Elijah the prophet arose like fire
p: Fire marks Elijah's story: fire on Carmel, fire on the soldiers, a chariot of fire. Manuscript B compares his words to a burning furnace.
b: Fire fell at Elijah's prayer on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) and on the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10–12), and a chariot of fire took him up (2 Kings 2:11). Manuscript B says 'his words were like a burning furnace' (ודבריו כתנור בוער), close to Malachi's day 'burning like an oven' (Malachi 4:1), the passage that promises Elijah's return (Malachi 4:5). When James and John wanted fire to come down on a Samaritan village, the Byzantine Greek text adds 'as Elijah did' (Luke 9:54).

a: He sent hunger on them
p: Elijah announced a drought that lasted until his contest on Carmel.
b: Elijah told Ahab, "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1). James 5:17 says that "for three years and six months no rain fell on the land" (James 5:17). Manuscript B says Elijah 'broke the staff of bread' for them, the curse of Leviticus 26:26.

a: called down fire three times
p: Fire fell once on Carmel and twice on the soldiers sent to arrest Elijah.
b: The first fire consumed Elijah's sacrifice on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). The second and third fell on two captains and their companies: "And fire came down out of the sky and devoured him and his fifty" (2 Kings 1:10; compare 2 Kings 1:12).

a: Hades
p: Hades is the Greek name for the world of the dead, the Septuagint's word for Sheol.
b: The Greek ᾅδου, Hades, translates the Hebrew Sheol, which manuscript B has here (ומשאול). It means the place of the dead, not a place of punishment. Elijah raised the widow's son at Zarephath: "The boy's life came back inside him, and he lived" (1 Kings 17:22). Hades comes again in 51:5–6.

a: brought the great down from their beds
p: Elijah foretold the end of Ahab's house and told King Ahaziah he would never rise from his sickbed.
b: Elijah pronounced doom on Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21:19–24). When King Ahaziah lay injured and sent to the god of Ekron, Elijah told him he would not get down from the bed he had gone up on (2 Kings 1:4, 16–17).

a: At Sinai you heard a rebuke
p: Sinai and Horeb are two names for the same mountain, set side by side as poetry.
b: Elijah fled to Horeb, the mountain of God, where God spoke in 'a quiet, thin sound' and sent him back with new orders (1 Kings 19:8–18). Ben Sira calls the meeting 'a rebuke' and the orders 'judgments of punishment': Hazael, Jehu and Elisha were to strike the house of Ahab and the worshipers of Baal.

a: You anointed kings to repay wrongs
p: God told Elijah to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha. Kings tells how it was done by others.
b: At Horeb God told Elijah to anoint Hazael king of Aram, Jehu king of Israel and Elisha as prophet (1 Kings 19:15–16). Elijah himself only threw his cloak over Elisha (1 Kings 19:19). Elisha told Hazael he would be king (2 Kings 8:13), and one of the sons of the prophets anointed Jehu (2 Kings 9:1–6). Ben Sira credits Elijah with what God told him to do and his successors carried out; here he goes beyond the story as Kings tells it, without contradicting its sense.

a: A whirlwind of fire carried you up
p: Elijah did not die but was taken up in a windstorm.
b: "Then, look, a chariot of fire and horses of fire came between the two of them, and Elijah went up to the heavens in the windstorm" (2 Kings 2:11). 1 Maccabees 2:58 says Elijah "was taken up as if into heaven" (1 Maccabees 2:58). Where Elijah went, and whether he returns in person, is asked on the card at 2 Kings 2.

a: You were written down in warnings for the times to come
p: Ben Sira is the earliest writer outside the prophets to take up Malachi's promise that Elijah will return.
b: The last words of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible are: "Look, I am about to send you Elijah the prophet before the day of the LORD comes, the great and awesome day" and "He will turn the hearts of fathers back to their sons" (Malachi 4:5–6; in Hebrew Bibles Malachi 3:23–24). Ben Sira says Elijah is 'written down' for this: he knows Malachi as Scripture. Manuscript B has להשיב לב אבות על בנים, 'to turn the heart of fathers to sons', in Malachi's plural; the Greek has the singular. Luke 1:17 applies the words to John the Baptist: "He will turn fathers' hearts back to their children" (Luke 1:17). Whether John fulfilled the promise or Elijah is still to come is the card at Malachi 4.

a: to set the tribes of Jacob on their feet
t: Elijah takes on the servant's task
p: Ben Sira adds to Malachi a task from Isaiah 49: Elijah will restore the tribes of Jacob.
b: In Isaiah the servant of the LORD is sent "to set the tribes of Jacob on their feet" (Isaiah 49:6). Ben Sira gives that work to the returning Elijah, so that Elijah will gather scattered Israel. Manuscript B has 'to prepare the tribes of Israel' (ולהכין שבטי ישראל). The disciples' question in Acts 1:6, whether Jesus would now restore the kingdom to Israel, comes from the same hope. Jesus' answer about Elijah, "Yes, Elijah is coming, and he will set everything right again" (Matthew 17:11), uses the language of restoring.

a: Happy those who saw you
t: A hard verse: who is happy?
p: The verse is uncertain in every witness. It may bless those who saw Elijah and died, or those who will see him return.
b: Swete's Greek reads 'Happy those who saw you and those adorned by love, for we too will live a true life.' Manuscript B is torn: its first words are אשר ראך, 'happy is he who saw you', then a word that may be 'and died' (ומת), and the rest is lost (Abegg and Parker restore 'before he dies' and, at the end, 'we shall live'). The KJV has 'and slept in love', from a Greek text that read 'fell asleep'. The Latin turns the end into a denial: 'For we live only in life; after death our name will not be such' (see the variant). Some read it as hope that those who die in love will live again; others as a blessing on those who will see Elijah come back. Given the book's silence on resurrection (44:9), the second reading is the more cautious.

a: his spirit filled Elisha
p: Elisha asked for a double share of Elijah's spirit. Manuscript B has a longer, damaged line about twofold signs.
b: "Please, let me have a double share of your spirit" (2 Kings 2:9). Manuscript B adds a line, mostly lost, that ends 'and wonders were every word that came from his mouth' (ומופתים כל מוצא פיהו). Elisha stood up to kings (2 Kings 3:13–14; 6:31–32), so 'no ruler made him tremble'.

a: even asleep in death his body prophesied
p: A dead man came to life when he touched Elisha's bones. Ben Sira calls this a prophecy by Elisha's body.
b: "They threw the man into Elisha's grave. Down he went, and when he touched Elisha's bones he came to life and stood up on his feet" (2 Kings 13:21). Manuscript B puts it as 'from under him his flesh was created', meaning the dead man's body was made new. Whether Christians should honor the relics of saints, a practice that has long cited this story, is the card at 2 Kings 13.

a: Even so, the people would not repent
p: Not even Elijah and Elisha turned the north back, and Assyria scattered it.
b: Ben Sira follows the judgment of 2 Kings 17:13–18: God warned Israel through every prophet, and they would not listen. 'Only a small people remained' is Judah, still with a king of David's house, until it too fell (49:4–6).

a: Some of them did what was pleasing
t: Good and bad kings of Judah
p: Ben Sira judges Judah's kings as Kings does: some did right, others sinned more and more.
b: Kings sums up each king of Judah by whether he did right in the LORD's eyes. Manuscript B says 'some of them did what was upright, and some of them did outrageous wrong' (יש מהם עשו יושר). In 49:4 Ben Sira is sharper: only David, Hezekiah and Josiah escape blame.

a: With iron he cut through solid rock
p: Hezekiah brought water into Jerusalem through a tunnel cut in the rock, still visible today.
b: Kings says Hezekiah "made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city" (2 Kings 20:20), and Chronicles that he blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and brought the water down to the west side of the City of David (2 Chronicles 32:30). The tunnel, which still carries the spring's water to the Pool of Siloam, has an inscription carved by the workers telling how two crews tunneled from each end and met. Manuscript B has 'he hewed rocks like bronze' (ויחצב כנחשת צורים).

a: the Rabshakeh
p: The Rabshakeh was an Assyrian official, 'chief cupbearer'; the Greek treats the title as a name.
b: Kings names three Assyrian officials sent to Jerusalem: "the Tartan, the Rab-saris and the Rabshakeh" (2 Kings 18:17). Rab-shakeh means 'chief cupbearer', a senior officer. The Greek here writes Rhapsakēs like a personal name, and manuscript B has 'the Rabshakeh' (רב שקה). He shouted his threats in Hebrew from beneath the wall (2 Kings 18:19–35).

a: set them free through Isaiah's hand
p: Hezekiah prayed, and God answered through Isaiah's message.
b: Hezekiah spread the Assyrian letter before the LORD and prayed (2 Kings 19:14–19), and Isaiah sent God's answer: the king of Assyria would not enter the city (2 Kings 19:20–34; Isaiah 37:21–35). Manuscript B has 'he saved them by the hand of Isaiah' (ויושיעם ביד ישעיהו), a play on the prophet's name, which means 'the LORD saves'.

a: his angel destroyed them
p: An angel struck the Assyrian army in one night. Manuscript B says God routed them 'with a plague'.
b: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (2 Kings 19:35). Manuscript B has 'he routed them with a plague' (ויהמם במגפה), which readers have linked with a sudden epidemic.

a: the sun stepped back
p: God turned the shadow back ten steps as a sign that Hezekiah would recover.
b: "So the sun went back ten steps, on the steps where it had gone down" (Isaiah 38:8). Ben Sira uses the same Greek verb as for Joshua's sun in 46:4, so the hymn has two sun miracles. God added fifteen years to Hezekiah's life (2 Kings 20:6).

a: By a great spirit he saw the last things
p: Ben Sira credits Isaiah with the comfort for Zion of Isaiah 40–66. Readers draw different conclusions from this.
b: 'He comforted those who mourned in Zion' takes words from the later chapters of Isaiah: "Comfort, comfort my people" (Isaiah 40:1) and the anointed one sent "to comfort all who mourn" (Isaiah 61:2). Manuscript B has 'he comforted the mourners of Zion' (וינחם אבלי ציון), as in Isaiah 61:3. So by about 180 BC the whole book was read as Isaiah's. Those who hold that Isaiah wrote all sixty-six chapters see Ben Sira as an early witness. Most critical scholars hold that chapters 40–66 come from later prophets, and say Ben Sira shows only that the book was complete and read as one by his time. The topic page on Isaiah gives both views.

a: Josiah's memory is a mix of incense
p: Ben Sira uses three pleasant things to praise the reforming king: incense, honey and music at a feast.
b: Incense was made by a skilled blender: "Make it into incense, a blend mixed by the perfumer's art" (Exodus 30:35). Ben Sira also compares music at a wine banquet to a jewel set in gold (35:5–6). Josiah's reform cleansed the temple and restored the Passover (2 Kings 22–23). He died young at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29), and Jeremiah mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:25).

a: took away the abhorrent things of lawlessness
p: Josiah removed the idols and shrines from Judah.
b: 2 Kings 23:4–20 lists what Josiah destroyed: the objects for Baal and Asherah, the horses of the sun, the shrines from Solomon's time, and the altar at Bethel. Manuscript B begins differently: 'for he grieved over our turning away' (כי נחל על משובתינו).

a: Apart from David, Hezekiah and Josiah
p: Ben Sira is harder than Kings, which also praises Asa, Jehoshaphat and others, though with limits.
b: Kings says of Hezekiah, "Among all the kings of Judah, none after him was like him" (2 Kings 18:5), and of Josiah, "No king before him was like him" (2 Kings 23:25). It also says Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah and Jotham did right, though they left the high places standing (1 Kings 15:11–14; 22:43). Ben Sira keeps only the three with no such fault. Here he agrees with Kings' highest praise and goes beyond it in condemning the rest.

a: because of Jeremiah
p: Greek and Hebrew say 'by the hand of Jeremiah'. It can mean 'as Jeremiah foretold' or 'because of what they did to Jeremiah'.
b: The Greek ἐν χειρὶ Ἰερεμίου and manuscript B's ביד ירמיהו mean 'by the hand of Jeremiah'. In the Hebrew Bible 'by the hand of a prophet' usually means 'through his word'. But the next line explains: 'for they had done him harm' (in manuscript B, 'for they afflicted him', כי ענוהו). So Ben Sira links the city's fall with the people's treatment of the prophet (Jeremiah 37–38). The Plain gives that link.

a: though in the womb he was made holy as a prophet
p: Ben Sira quotes Jeremiah 1:5 and 1:10.
b: God told Jeremiah: "before you came out of the womb, I made you holy" (Jeremiah 1:5), and "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). Manuscript B has the full list of Jeremiah 1:10. The Greek uses one verb, kakoō, 'harm', both for what the people did to Jeremiah and for one of his tasks, a play the Plain keeps with 'harm'. Paul echoes the call in Galatians 1:15.

a: Ezekiel was shown a vision of glory
p: Ezekiel saw God's glory above the living creatures and wheels. Later Jewish teachers called this 'the Chariot' and guarded its study.
b: Ezekiel 1 and 10 describe the cherubim, the wheels and the throne: "That was the look of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (Ezekiel 1:28). Manuscript B says he 'told the kinds of the chariot' (ויגד זני מרכבה), using merkavah, 'chariot', which became the name of this vision in Jewish tradition. The Mishnah allows its study only to a wise person who understands on his own (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1).

a: did good to those who walk straight paths
p: Manuscript B names Job here. The Greek read the same Hebrew letters as 'enemy'.
b: Manuscript B, folio XVIII verso, line 14, reads 'and he also mentioned Job (איוב), the prophet, who held to all the ways of righteousness'. The point is that Ezekiel named Job among the righteous: "Noah, Daniel and Job" (Ezekiel 14:14). In Hebrew, Job (איוב) and 'enemy' (אויב) differ only in the order of two letters, and the Greek has 'he remembered the enemies' (τῶν ἐχθρῶν). 'With a downpour' may come from the storm of Ezekiel 13:11–13 and 38:22, or from a misreading. So Job, missing from the Greek, stands in the Hebrew list of the fathers.

a: the bones of the Twelve Prophets
t: The earliest witness to the Twelve
p: Ben Sira is the oldest writer known to speak of 'the Twelve Prophets' as one group, after Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
b: The Greek reads καὶ τῶν ιβ᾽ προφητῶν τὰ ὀστᾶ ἀναθάλοι ἐκ τοῦ τόπου αὐτῶν, 'and may the bones of the twelve prophets sprout from their place', with the number written as a Greek numeral (ιβ᾽); Codex Alexandrinus spells it out (δώδεκα). Manuscript B, folio XVIII verso, line 15, has וגם שנים עשר הנביאים, 'and also the Twelve Prophets', then תהי עצמתם 'may their bones' and a damaged word restored as 'sprout' (פר[חות]) 'from their place' (מתח[תם]). The order Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve is the order of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. So about 180 BC Hosea to Malachi were already one collection, the Book of the Twelve; Ben Sira has just quoted its last book (48:10).

a: like a seal ring on the right hand
p: Ben Sira echoes Haggai's promise to Zerubbabel, which reversed God's rejection of King Jehoiachin.
b: God said through Haggai: "I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, the LORD declares, and I will make you like a seal ring, for I have chosen you" (Haggai 2:23). Jeremiah had said that if King Coniah (Jehoiachin) "were the seal ring on my right hand, from that very spot I would pull you off" (Jeremiah 22:24). Zerubbabel was Jehoiachin's grandson, so the promise restored David's line. Ben Sira praises him but says nothing of a coming king.

a: Jeshua son of Jozadak was the same
p: Jeshua, the first high priest after the exile, rebuilt the altar and temple with Zerubbabel.
b: "Then Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up with his brothers the priests, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel with his brothers" (Ezra 3:2). Haggai calls him "Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest" (Haggai 1:1), and Zechariah saw him and Zerubbabel as "the two sons of fresh oil who stand by the Lord of the whole earth" (Zechariah 4:14). His Greek name is Iēsous, as in 46:1.

a: who lifted our fallen walls back up
p: Ben Sira praises Nehemiah for rebuilding the walls but never mentions Ezra, the scribe and teacher of the law.
b: Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's wall: "Come on, let's rebuild Jerusalem's wall, so we are not a laughingstock anymore" (Nehemiah 2:17). Ezra, the priest and scribe who brought the law from Babylon and read it to the people (Ezra 7; Nehemiah 8), would seem the perfect hero for a scribe like Ben Sira, yet he is missing. Readers have offered reasons: Ben Sira chose builders to lead up to Simon, the builder-priest (50:1–4); he knew Nehemiah's memoir better; or he was cool toward Ezra's hard line on foreign marriages (Ezra 9–10). None of these can be proved. 2 Maccabees 2:13 also remembers Nehemiah, as a founder of a library.

a: No one like Enoch was ever made on earth
p: Ben Sira returns to Enoch. Manuscript B says 'few' were made like him, and that he was 'taken inside'.
b: After Nehemiah, the hymn goes back to the start of the human story: Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth and Adam (49:14–16). Manuscript B has 'few on the earth were made like Enoch' and 'he too was taken inward' (נלקח פנים), perhaps 'into the presence'. Enoch's taking (Genesis 5:24) was much discussed in Ben Sira's time, as 1 Enoch shows.

a: his bones were watched over
p: Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan, and they did.
b: "Joseph had the sons of Israel take an oath: 'God will surely come to help you. When he does, carry my bones up from here.'" (Genesis 50:25). Moses took them (Exodus 13:19) and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). The Greek verb 'watched over' is the same as 'come to help' (see 46:14). Hebrews 11:22 counts Joseph's instruction about his bones as faith.

a: but above every living thing in creation is Adam
p: Ben Sira ends the line of heroes with Adam honored above all creation, and says nothing here of his sin.
b: Manuscript B has 'Shem, Seth and Enosh were cared for, and above every living thing is the glory of Adam' (ועל כל חי תפארת אדם). The Greek leaves out Enosh. Ben Sira honors Adam as God's creature, made from the dust and given life (Genesis 2:7; 17:1–4). In 25:24 he blames the beginning of sin on a woman, and Wisdom says that wisdom "pulled him out of his own trespass" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:1). Paul traces sin and death to Adam (Romans 5:12) and contrasts him with Christ (1 Corinthians 15:45). Here Ben Sira stresses Adam's dignity, not his fall.
r: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 4:25–26; 17:1–4; 25:24; Wisdom of Solomon 10:1; Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 15:45

a: Simon son of Onias, the high priest
p: Most historians identify him with Simon II, high priest about 200 BC. Josephus calls an earlier Simon 'the Just'.
b: Josephus says that when an Onias died, "left the high priesthood to his son Simeon" (Antiquities 12.224, in Whiston's translation), in the time of Antiochus III, around 200 BC. This Simon II fits Ben Sira's date and his building work (see 50:2–4). Josephus also gives the title 'the Just' to an earlier Simon, son of Onias I (Antiquities 12.43), and the Mishnah remembers 'Shimon the Righteous' as one of the last of the Men of the Great Assembly, who taught that the world stands on the Torah, the temple service and acts of loving kindness (Mishnah Avot 1:2). Which Simon the rabbis meant is debated. Manuscript B calls him 'Simon son of Yohanan' and first says he was 'the greatest of his brothers and the glory of his people' (see the variant). His son Onias III is the godly high priest of 2 Maccabees 3:1.

a: mended the house while he lived
t: Repairs after the war of 200 BC
p: Antiochus III, after taking Judea from Egypt, ordered that the work on the temple be finished, which fits Simon's repairs.
b: Around 200 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus III took Judea from the Ptolemies of Egypt. Josephus quotes his letter, which says the Jews "joined with us in ejecting the garrison of the Egyptians that were in the citadel" (Antiquities 12.138, Whiston), and orders "the work about the temple finished, and the cloisters", with timber brought tax-free (Antiquities 12.141, Whiston). Ben Sira's picture of Simon repairing the house, building walls and strengthening the city (50:1–4) matches that time of rebuilding after war.

a: a bronze basin as round as the sea
p: The Greek compares the new reservoir to bronze and to the sea, recalling Solomon's great bronze Sea.
b: Solomon's temple had a huge bronze basin called 'the Sea' (1 Kings 7:23–26). Swete's Greek says the reservoir was 'bronze like a sea in circumference'; Codex Alexandrinus has 'a cistern' (lakkos) instead of 'bronze' (chalkos), a one-letter difference in Greek. Manuscript B has 'a pool like the sea in its abundance' (אשיח בם בהמונו). Water for washing was vital to the temple's work, and Jerusalem had few springs.

a: strengthened the city to hold out under siege
p: Jerusalem had just come through a war between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids.
b: Judea changed hands more than once in the wars between Egypt and Syria in the late 200s BC. Simon's care to keep his people 'from falling' and to fortify the city reflects that danger. Manuscript B says he 'cared for his people against robbery' and 'strengthened his city against the enemy'.

a: when he stepped out from the house of the curtain
t: The Day of Atonement or the daily offering?
p: Readers disagree whether Ben Sira describes Simon on the Day of Atonement or at the daily offering.
b: Manuscript B says Simon was glorious 'when he looked out from the tent and when he came out from the house of the curtain' (ובצאתו מבית הפרכת). The Day of Atonement: only on that day did the high priest pass behind the inner curtain (Leviticus 16:2, 12–15; Mishnah Yoma 5:1), so his coming out suggests Yom Kippur; the Yom Kippur poem 'Mareh Kohen', 'the appearance of the priest', still sung in the additional service, echoes this chapter. The daily offering: what follows (50:12–21) matches the Mishnah's account of the daily burnt offering when the high priest took part: he takes the pieces at the altar, pours the wine, two priests blow silver trumpets, the Levites sing and the people fall prostrate (Mishnah Tamid 7:3), and the priests bless the people (Mishnah Tamid 7:2). Nothing in Sirach 50 mentions the goats or the sprinkling of blood. Some see a picture drawn from many occasions.

a: He was like the star of dawn between clouds
t: Simon among the lights and trees
p: Ben Sira piles up images of sky, flowers, trees and temple vessels, many of them used of Wisdom in chapter 24.
b: Simon is star, moon, sun and rainbow (50:6–7), rose, lily, Lebanon's growth (50:8), incense and gold (50:9), olive and cypress (50:10). In chapter 24 Wisdom compares herself to the cedar of Lebanon, the cypress, the palm, the rose, the olive and sweet spices (24:13–15), and says she ministered before God in the holy tent in Zion (24:10). Read together, the high priest at the altar looks like Wisdom at home in the temple. The Yom Kippur poem 'Mareh Kohen' echoes this chapter's picture of the high priest.

a: like the bow that lights up the glorious clouds
p: The rainbow recalls Noah's covenant and Ezekiel's vision of God's glory.
b: Ezekiel saw God's glory "Like the look of the bow that is in the clouds on a day of rain" (Ezekiel 1:28), and the rainbow is the sign of God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:13). Revelation 4:3 sets a rainbow around God's throne.

a: like fire and frankincense in the fire pan
p: Incense was burned on the golden altar every morning and evening.
b: Aaron was to burn incense every morning and at dusk (Exodus 30:7–8). Manuscript B has 'like the fire of frankincense on the grain offering', the frankincense laid on the grain offering of Leviticus 2:1–2. Psalm 141:2 asks that prayer rise like incense.

a: dressed in the fullness of splendor
p: The Greek phrase is the same one used for Aaron's vestments in 45:8.
b: 'The fullness of splendor' renders συντέλειαν καυχήματος, the very words of 45:8. Ben Sira dresses Simon in the clothes he described for Aaron: the high priest of his own day is Aaron's living heir. Manuscript B speaks of 'garments of glory' and 'garments of beauty' (בגדי כבוד, בגדי תפארת), the phrase of Exodus 28:2.

a: As he took the pieces of the sacrifice from the priests' hands
p: The Mishnah describes the same scene: priests hand the high priest the pieces, and he throws them on the altar fire.
b: In the Mishnah's account of the daily offering, the high priest goes up the ramp to the altar, the priests hand him the head, legs and other pieces one after another, and he lays his hands on them and throws them on the fire (Mishnah Tamid 7:3). Ben Sira's 'portions' (melē, 'limbs') are those pieces. The other priests stand around him like young cedars and palm trees, trees that also stand for the righteous in Psalm 92:12.

a: the Lord's offering
p: Manuscript B has 'the LORD's offerings by fire', the priestly term for gifts burned on the altar.
b: Manuscript B reads 'and the LORD's offerings by fire (אשי ייי) in their hands, before the whole assembly of Israel'. 'Offering by fire' is the term of Leviticus 2:2. The Greek has the general word prosphora, 'offering'.

a: poured out some of the grape's blood
p: Wine was poured out with the daily offering. Manuscript B has no line for this verse.
b: A drink offering of wine went with each daily lamb (Exodus 29:40; Numbers 28:7). 'The blood of the grape' is old poetry: Jacob's blessing on Judah speaks of "his robe in the blood of grapes" (Genesis 49:11). The Mishnah says the high priest poured the wine at a corner of the altar, and at that moment the Levites began to sing (Mishnah Tamid 7:3). Manuscript B passes straight from 50:14 to 50:16 (folio XIX verso, lines 7–8).

a: sounded the beaten-metal trumpets
p: Numbers 10 commands two hammered silver trumpets, blown over the offerings as a reminder before God.
b: "Make yourself two trumpets of silver. Make them of hammered work" (Numbers 10:2). They were blown over the offerings: "Then they will call you to mind before your God" (Numbers 10:10). Ben Sira's 'for a reminder before the Most High' is that purpose. The Mishnah has two priests with silver trumpets at the daily offering (Mishnah Tamid 7:3).

a: fell face down on the ground
p: The Mishnah says the people bowed down at every trumpet blast during the Levites' song.
b: At the daily offering, the Mishnah says, the Levites sang the psalm of the day in three sections, the priests blew a blast at the end of each, and at every blast the people bowed down (Mishnah Tamid 7:3). On the Day of Atonement the people fell on their faces whenever they heard the high priest say the divine Name (Mishnah Yoma 6:2). The scene also recalls 2 Chronicles 29:28–29.

a: before the Merciful One
p: Ben Sira uses 'the Merciful One' as a name of God.
b: The Greek has Ἐλεήμονος, 'the Merciful One', and manuscript B has rachum (רחום), the first word of God's self-description in Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious'.

a: to speak the Lord's blessing with his lips
t: The Priestly Blessing, with the Name
p: Simon comes down and blesses the people with raised hands, as Aaron did. Manuscript B and the Mishnah suggest the divine name was spoken.
b: Aaron did the same at his first offering: "Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them. Then he came down from offering" (Leviticus 9:22). The blessing is the one of Numbers 6: "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24). Manuscript B has 'the blessing of the LORD on his lips, and in the name of the LORD he gloried' (וברכת ייי בשפתיו). The Mishnah says that in the temple the priests said the name as it is written, while elsewhere they used a substitute (Mishnah Tamid 7:2). 'To take pride in his name' may mean Simon spoke the Name itself.

a: the one who does great things everywhere
p: These verses inspired one of the best-known Protestant hymns, written by a Lutheran pastor during the Thirty Years' War.
b: Martin Rinkart, a Lutheran pastor in Saxony, wrote 'Nun danket alle Gott' about 1636, based on 50:22–24; Catherine Winkworth's English is 'Now Thank We All Our God'. Rinkart followed the Greek text the KJV also used, 'Now therefore bless ye the God of all, which only doeth wondrous things every where' (KJV). The hymn shows how Sirach, which Lutherans did not count as Scripture, still shaped Protestant prayer.
