Now Thank We All Our God

a: and may he set us free in his time
p: In the Hebrew Ben Sira prays for Simon and his line. His grandson's Greek, made after that line had lost the office, prays for 'us'.
b: Manuscript B prays: 'May his loyal love stay faithful to Simon, and may he keep for him the covenant of Phinehas, never to be cut off for him or his offspring as long as the heavens last' (see the variant). The Greek, translated after 132 BC, asks instead that God's mercy stay with 'us'. By then Simon's family had lost the high priesthood: his son Onias III was murdered (2 Maccabees 4:34), the office was bought and sold (2 Maccabees 4:7–26), and from 152 BC the Hasmoneans held it (1 Maccabees 10:20–21). One likely reason for the change is that the prayer for Simon's line could no longer be prayed as written.

a: There are two nations I loathe with all my soul
p: Ben Sira uses a 'two and three' pattern, a teaching form found in Proverbs.
b: Sayings that count up ('There are three things... four') are common in Proverbs 30:15–31 and in Ben Sira (25:1–2, 7; 26:5, 28). Here two nations and a third that is 'no nation at all' build to the climax: the people of Shechem.

a: the foolish people who live in Shechem
p: 'The foolish people who live in Shechem' are the Samaritans, who worshiped on Mount Gerizim above Shechem.
b: In Ben Sira's day the Samaritans had their own temple on Mount Gerizim, above Shechem, rival to Jerusalem's. Manuscript B calls them goy naval, the 'foolish nation' of Deuteronomy, where God says he will "anger them with a nation of fools" (Deuteronomy 32:21): a people that is not a real people. The Greek 'hill of Samaria' stands where manuscript B has Seir, the land of Edom (see the variant); either way the three are neighbors on three sides of Judea. The hostility is the one behind John 4:9, 'Jews do not associate with Samaritans', which Jesus crossed (John 4; Luke 10:33).

a: In this book I have engraved instruction
p: In this part the Greek paideia is 'instruction': schooling in wisdom, not punishment.
b: Παιδείαν can mean training, education or discipline. Where it means a learner's schooling, as here and in 51:16, 23, 26 and 28, this part renders it 'instruction'; manuscript B has musar, the 'discipline' of Proverbs 1:2. The verb 'engraved' (echaraxa) is used for cutting letters into stone or wax. This verse is the author's signature, the only place the book names him.

a: who rained down wisdom from his heart
p: The Greek pictures wisdom pouring from his heart like rain.
b: The Greek verb ἀνώμβρησεν means 'poured out like a rainstorm'. Manuscript B has 'who poured out in the explanation of his heart' (אשר ניבע בפתור לבן). Ben Sira uses water for teaching elsewhere: the law overflows with wisdom like rivers, and he is a canal from the river (24:25–31).

a: Happy is the one who lives among these words
t: Happy is the one who meditates
p: The blessing echoes Psalm 1, but for Ben Sira's own book.
b: "Instead, the law of the LORD is his delight, / and he murmurs over his law day and night" (Psalm 1:2). Ben Sira promises the same happiness to whoever lives with his teaching. Manuscript B: 'Happy the man who meditates on these' (באלה יהגה), the verb of Psalm 1:2.

a: A prayer of Jesus son of Sirach.
p: The Greek gives the prayer a title; manuscript B has none and begins at once.
b: The Greek heading Προσευχὴ Ἰησοῦ υἱοῦ Σειράχ marks the chapter as a separate piece. Manuscript B runs on from 50:29 on the same line and begins 'I will praise you, God of my salvation' (אהללך אלהי ישעי). The prayer is a song of thanks for rescue, like Psalm 18 or Psalm 30. 'God, my Savior' is also Mary's phrase: "my spirit has found its gladness in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47).
orig: Προσευχὴ Ἰησοῦ υἱοῦ Σειράχ (proseuchē Iēsou huiou Seirach)

a: from the snare of a slandering tongue
t: A real danger, or the language of the Psalms?
p: Ben Sira speaks of slander, a king and near death. It may be his own story or the stock language of thanksgiving psalms.
b: He thanks God for rescue from lies told about him to a king (51:6), from enemies who surrounded him and from near death. In 31:12–13 he says he was often in danger of death on his travels and escaped. Some read chapter 51 as a record of a real accusation before a foreign ruler. Others note that every phrase has parallels in the Psalms (Psalm 18:4–6; 31:13; 120:2) and read it as the model prayer of a wise man. Both can be true.

a: from fire that choked me on every side
p: The fire may be a picture of danger, as in Isaiah 43:2, or recall Daniel's friends in the furnace.
b: Isaiah promises, when you walk through fire you will not be burned (Isaiah 43:2), and Psalm 66:12 says 'we went through fire and through water'. Daniel 3 tells of three young men kept safe in a furnace. Ben Sira's 'flames I had not lit' means trouble he had not caused.

a: from deep in Hades' belly
p: Jonah prayed from 'the belly of Sheol'.
b: Jonah prayed: "From the belly of Sheol I cried for help; / you heard my voice" (Jonah 2:2). Ben Sira uses the same picture of being as good as dead; manuscript B has 'from the womb of the deep' (מרחם תהום).

a: the Father of my lord
p: The Greek calls on 'the Lord, the Father of my lord'. Christians heard Christ in the words; manuscript B has 'You are my Father'.
b: The Greek Kyrion patera kyriou mou calls God 'Lord, father of my lord'. Christian readers heard here the language of Psalm 110:1, "The LORD declares to my lord" (Psalm 110:1), which Jesus applied to himself (Matthew 22:41–45), so that Ben Sira seems to call on the Father of the Lord Jesus. Manuscript B reads 'I exalted the LORD: You are my Father' (וארומם ייי אבי אתה), the words of Psalm 89:26, "You are my Father, / my God, the rock of my rescue" (Psalm 89:26). Many think the Greek doubled 'Lord' by mistake or by a reading of the Hebrew. Ben Sira also calls God 'Father' in 23:1 and 23:4. The KJV prints 'the Father of my Lord' with a capital (KJV).

a: And my plea was heard
p: Like many psalms, the prayer moves from need to thanks: God heard.
b: Compare "The LORD has heard my plea for grace" (Psalm 6:9) and Psalm 28:6. Manuscript B: 'Then the LORD heard my voice and listened to my pleading' (אז שמע קולי ייי).

a: and bless the Lord's name
p: Manuscript B adds a sixteen-line litany of thanks, like Psalm 136. The Greek, the Latin and the KJV do not have it.
b: In manuscript B (folio XX verso, line 12, to XXI recto, line 8) this verse is followed by a psalm translated here from the Hebrew: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, / for his loyal love is forever" (Psalm 136:1). Then, each with the refrain 'for his loyal love is forever': give thanks to the God of praises; to the guardian of Israel; to the maker of all; to the redeemer of Israel; to the one who gathers Israel's scattered people; to the one who builds his city and his sanctuary; הודו למצמיח קרן לבית דוד, to the one who makes a horn sprout for the house of David; to the one who chose the sons of Zadok to be priests; to the shield of Abraham; to the rock of Isaac; to the mighty one of Jacob; to the one who chose Zion; to the King of the kings of kings. It ends like Psalm 148:14: 'He has raised a horn for his people, praise for all his loyal ones, for the Israelites, the people near him. Hallelujah.' Whether Ben Sira wrote it or a later copyist added it is debated; the line on the sons of Zadok would suit a time before the Hasmoneans took the high priesthood.

a: When I was still a youth, before I went wandering
t: An alphabet poem, found at Qumran
p: 51:13–30 was in Hebrew an acrostic, one line for each letter of the alphabet. Part of it was found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran.
b: In Hebrew each couplet of this poem began with the next letter of the alphabet. The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11QPs-a), copied in the first century, has 51:13–20 and the last words of 51:30 in its columns XXI–XXII, among the psalms. It begins אני נער בטרם תעיתי ובקשתיה, 'I was a young man before I went astray, and I sought her', with aleph, the first letter. Manuscript B also has the poem, but its alphabet order is broken in places. Because the poem stands in a psalm collection, some think it circulated on its own before it was attached to Sirach. The Greek cannot show the alphabet.

a: before I went wandering
p: The Greek verb can mean 'travel' or 'go astray'; the Qumran Hebrew has 'before I went astray'.
b: The Greek πρὶν ἢ πλανηθῆναί με can mean 'before I traveled' (Ben Sira speaks of his travels in 31:12) or 'before I strayed'. 11QPs-a has ta'iti, 'I went astray', and 'I was a young man' (אני נער). The Plain keeps 'wandering', which can carry both.

a: Facing the temple I pleaded for her
p: 11QPs-a has 'she came to me in her beauty' instead of praying before the temple.
b: For the second line of the poem, the letter bet, 11QPs-a reads באה לי בתרה, 'she came to me in her beauty', and goes on 'and to her end I will search for her'. The Greek has the young man praying before the temple. The Qumran wording, here and in the lines that follow, speaks of wisdom more like a beloved, as Ben Sira also does in 14:20–27 and 15:2.

a: From flower to ripening grape
p: The young man watched wisdom grow from blossom to ripe grape.
b: Wisdom calls herself a vine in 24:17, and the Song of Songs uses blossoming vines for young love (Song of Songs 2:13; 7:12). 11QPs-a has 'the blossom fell, as in the ripening of grapes, which gladden the heart'.
r: 24:17; Song of Songs 2:13; Song of Songs 7:12

a: Through her I went forward
p: Manuscript B and the Qumran scroll speak of wisdom's 'yoke' here, the word that returns in 51:26.
b: The Greek has prokopē, 'progress'. Manuscript B reads 'her yoke (עלה) was glory to me', and 11QPs-a has a similar word. If 'yoke' is right, the poem uses the same image twice: here the young man accepts wisdom's yoke, and in 51:26 he invites others to put their necks under it.

a: Deep inside I was stirred
p: The Greek says 'my belly was stirred'; manuscript B, 'my insides roar like an oven'.
b: The Greek koilia, 'belly', is the seat of deep feeling. Manuscript B has מעי יהמו כתנור, 'my insides roar like an oven', the language of longing in Song of Songs 5:4 and Jeremiah 4:19.

a: stay in the house of instruction
p: Manuscript B has 'my house of study', beit midrash, the phrase that later named the Jewish study hall.
b: The Greek oikos paideias means 'house of instruction'. Manuscript B reads פנו אלי סכלים ולינו בבית מדרשי, 'turn to me, you fools, and lodge in my house of study'. Beit midrash became the name of the place where Jews study Torah. The 'untaught' are students like those Ben Sira calls 'my child' throughout the book. Wisdom gave a similar invitation: "Come, have some of my bread, / and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5).

a: Get her for yourselves without paying silver.
p: Ben Sira's offer recalls Isaiah 55:1.
b: "Come, buy without money, without a price, / wine and milk" (Isaiah 55:1). Wisdom is free, yet 51:28 says it is worth paying silver for. Manuscript B: 'buy wisdom for yourselves without silver' (קנו לכם חכמה בלא כסף).

a: Bend your neck under the yoke
t: The yoke and rest: Sirach and Matthew 11
p: Ben Sira's invitation to take on wisdom's yoke and find rest has close parallels in Jesus' words in Matthew 11:28–30.
b: Ben Sira calls the untaught to come to him (51:23), to put their necks under the yoke (51:26) and see that he 'toiled a little and found great rest' (51:27). Jesus says: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), and "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me" (Matthew 11:29). Many Christian readers see Jesus speaking as Wisdom in person (compare Matthew 11:19). Jewish teachers spoke of 'the yoke of the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 3:5), and Ben Sira's yoke is wisdom found in the law (6:24–30; 24:23). The shared words are clear; whether Matthew draws on Sirach or both draw on common wisdom language is debated.

a: found great rest for myself
p: Rest is wisdom's reward, as in Jeremiah 6:16 and Matthew 11:29.
b: Jesus promises "And you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29), from Jeremiah 6:16. Ben Sira says wisdom gives rest at the end (6:28). Manuscript B: 'see with your eyes that I was small and stood in her and found her'.

a: Pay a large sum of silver for instruction
p: The Greek says instruction is worth a high price; manuscript B says students heard him and gained silver and gold.
b: Manuscript B has 'many heard my teaching in my youth, and you will gain silver and gold through me' (רבים שמעו למודי בנערותי). Proverbs says wisdom is better than silver and gold (Proverbs 3:14; 8:10, 19), and Ben Sira joins the two ideas: spend on it and it repays you.

a: he will give you your reward in his own time
t: How the book ends in the manuscripts
p: Manuscript B ends with a signature and a blessing; the Greek manuscripts end with the title 'Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach'.
b: 11QPs-a also ends the poem with 'your reward in its time' (שכרכם בעתו, column XXII, line 1). Manuscript B adds 'Blessed be the LORD forever' and then: עד הנה דברי שמעון בן ישוע שנקרא בן סירא, 'Up to here are the words of Simeon son of Jeshua, who is called Ben Sira', followed by 'The Wisdom of Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira' and 'May the name of the LORD be blessed from now to forever.' Swete's notes give the closing title in Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus as 'Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach'. That is where the book's Greek name comes from.
